title: Islam, Byzantium and Africa
bigQuestion: How did faith, law and trade tie together cities as far apart as Constantinople, Baghdad and Timbuktu?

story.title: The King Who Broke the Price of Gold
story.kicker: In the summer of 1324 a ruler from West Africa rode into Cairo with so much gold that the city talked about him for years.
paragraphs: The guards on the walls of Cairo saw the dust first. Then the line of camels came into view, and it did not end. Riders in fine cloth, servants on foot, soldiers with spears, and camel after camel loaded with bags. Inside the bags was gold dust. At the center of it all rode Mansa Musa, the ruler of the Empire of Mali, a land far to the southwest across the Sahara Desert. He was on his way to Mecca, the holy city of Islam, to make the pilgrimage every Muslim hopes to make once in life.

Cairo in 1324 was one of the biggest cities in the world, and its people had seen many rich visitors. They had never seen this. Mansa Musa gave gold to the officials who greeted him. He gave gold to the poor at the mosques. His followers bought silk, horses and slaves, and paid whatever price the sellers named. Gold poured into the markets faster than anyone could count it.

Here is what the merchants of Cairo learned the hard way. When there is suddenly a great deal of something, each piece of it is worth less. So much gold entered Cairo that summer that the price of gold fell. A writer named al-Umari, who talked to people in Cairo a few years later, reported that the value of gold there stayed low for more than ten years. One traveler's generosity had bent the economy of a great city.

Why does this story matter? Because it shows a world we do not always picture. In the year 1324, a Muslim king from West Africa could travel thousands of miles through Muslim lands, speaking to scholars in Arabic, using the same calendar and the same prayers, welcomed as a fellow believer. The desert that looks empty on a map was a highway. Gold, salt, books and ideas moved across it. This chapter follows that road, from the marble churches of Constantinople to the mud-brick libraries of Timbuktu.
story.think: Mansa Musa gave away gold to be generous and to show his power. What did Cairo gain from his visit, and what did it lose?

sections.title: The Empire That Did Not Fall

lessons.title: A City Between Two Seas
lessons.mainIdea: When Rome's western half collapsed, its eastern half lived on for a thousand years from Constantinople, a city built on a narrow strait.
reading: In the year 330 the Roman emperor Constantine chose a new capital. He picked an old Greek town on a narrow strip of water where Europe almost touches Asia. He renamed it after himself: Constantinople. The place was easy to defend and hard to starve. Water surrounded it on three sides, and thick walls closed the fourth. Ships from the Black Sea and the Mediterranean had to pass right beside it, and each one paid a tax.

In 476 the last Roman emperor in the West lost his throne, and the western empire broke into small kingdoms. The eastern half did not break. Its people still called themselves Romans, but historians call their state the *Byzantine* Empire, after Byzantium, the old name of the city. It lasted from 330 until 1453, more than eleven hundred years. Its people spoke Greek, kept Roman law and followed Christianity.

Constantinople was the largest city in Europe for most of that time, with perhaps several hundred thousand people. Its markets sold silk from China, furs from Russia, spices from India and grain from Egypt. Its gold coin, the solidus, was so trusted that merchants used it from Britain to India. A traveler in the year 1000 who wanted to see the richest city in the Christian world went to Constantinople, not Rome or Paris.

How do we know? The walls still stand in the city now called Istanbul, in Turkey. Byzantine writers left histories, law books and church records. Coins turn up in graves as far away as Sweden. And the city's enemies wrote about it too, from Arab armies who failed to take it to Vikings who came to serve as the emperor's guards.

words.d: the name historians give the eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, 330 to 1453
a narrow strip of water that connects two larger bodies of water
the city where a government is based

look.title: Reading the Map
look.text: Picture Constantinople on a map. To the north, the Black Sea. To the south, the Mediterranean. The only water road between them runs past the city's docks. Every trading ship going either way must stop, pay a fee and perhaps sell some cargo.
look.prompt: How would this location help the city grow rich even in years when its armies were losing?

check.q: Why did Constantine choose the site of Constantinople?
choices: It had the best farmland in the empire
Water protected three sides and ships had to pass by it
It was the birthplace of Christianity
It was far from any sea
check.why: The city sat on a strait, so it was easy to defend and collected taxes from passing ships.

check.q: What happened to the Roman Empire in 476?
choices: The eastern half fell but the West survived
The western half fell but the East continued
The empire moved its capital to Rome
check.why: The West broke into kingdoms, while the eastern half, the Byzantine Empire, lasted until 1453.

check.q: Which is evidence that Byzantine coins were trusted far away?
choices: Byzantine coins have been found in graves in Sweden
The coins were made of silver
check.why: Coins found far from the empire show that distant merchants accepted and kept them.

lessons.title: Justinian Writes Down the Law
lessons.mainIdea: Emperor Justinian collected a thousand years of Roman law into one clear code, and that code still shapes laws in much of the world.
reading: Justinian became emperor in 527. He was born a peasant's son in the Balkans and rose through his uncle, who was a soldier and then emperor. Justinian wanted to make the empire great again. He sent armies to take back Italy and North Africa. He built churches and fortresses. But his most lasting project was quieter. He ordered a team of lawyers to fix the law.

The problem was a mess. Rome had made laws for a thousand years. Some contradicted others. Some were lost, and some lay buried in thousands of pages of old court opinions. A judge could not know which rule applied. Justinian's lawyers, led by a scholar named Tribonian, read through it all. Between 529 and 534 they produced a set of books that we call the *Code of Justinian*, or the Body of Civil Law.

The Code did three things. It threw out laws that no longer made sense. It sorted the rest by topic, so a judge could find the rule on, say, selling a house. And it added a short textbook for law students that began with a definition of justice: giving each person what is due to them. The books were written in Latin, the old language of Rome, even though most people in the empire now spoke Greek.

Centuries later, scholars in Italy rediscovered the Code and taught it in the first universities. Its ideas spread through France, Spain, Germany and their colonies. Today the legal systems of most of Europe and Latin America, and of the state of Louisiana, still trace back to Justinian's books. A person reading a contract in Mexico City or Paris is using rules a Byzantine emperor had written down.

words.d: a complete, organized set of laws written down in one place
to say the opposite of something else
the law about ordinary matters between people: property, contracts, marriage, debts

look.title: The First Lesson for Law Students
look.text: The student textbook in Justinian's Code opens by saying that justice is the steady and lasting will to give every person what is rightfully theirs. It then says the study of law has three basic rules: live honestly, harm no one, and give each person their due.
look.cite: Institutes of Justinian, opening section, about 533 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Which of the three rules would be hardest for a government to enforce, and why?

check.q: What problem was Justinian's Code meant to solve?
choices: The empire had no laws at all
Roman laws were scattered, lost or contradicted each other
The laws were written in Greek
check.why: A thousand years of Roman law had piled up in confusion, so the Code sorted, trimmed and organized it.

check.q: Which fact best shows the Code's long-term influence?
choices: Legal systems in Europe and Latin America still trace back to it
check.why: The Code was rediscovered in Italy and spread through Europe and its colonies, including Louisiana.

check.q: Why might it matter that the Code was in Latin while people spoke Greek?
choices: Latin had no words for law
Ordinary people could not easily read their own laws
Greek was banned in the empire
Latin was only spoken in Africa
check.why: Writing the law in a language most people did not use kept it in the hands of trained experts.

lessons.title: A Dome That Seemed to Float
lessons.mainIdea: Hagia Sophia showed the wealth and faith of Byzantium, and the split between its Greek church and Rome's Latin church still divides Christians today.
reading: In January 532 a riot nearly ended Justinian's reign. Crowds in Constantinople burned half the city, including the main church. The emperor packed to flee. His wife, the empress Theodora, told him she would rather die as a ruler than run. Justinian stayed, his soldiers crushed the riot, and he decided to rebuild the church bigger than anything on earth.

The new church was *Hagia Sophia*, which means Holy Wisdom in Greek. Two mathematicians designed it. Ten thousand workers finished it in under six years, in 537. Its great dome spans more than a hundred feet and rises about 180 feet above the floor. Forty windows circle the base of the dome, so sunlight pours in and the dome appears to hang in the air. Gold mosaics, tiny glass tiles, covered the walls. A writer of the time said visitors felt the building was not made by human hands.

Hagia Sophia was the center of the Eastern Orthodox Church, the Christianity of the Greek-speaking world. Its leader was the patriarch of Constantinople. Far to the west, the pope in Rome led the Latin-speaking church. The two churches prayed in different languages, argued about the wording of beliefs and about who was in charge. In 1054 their leaders formally split. That break is called the *schism*, and the Orthodox and Catholic churches remain separate to this day.

The Byzantines sent missionaries north. Two brothers, Cyril and Methodius, made an alphabet for the Slavic peoples in the 800s. Russia, Serbia, Bulgaria and Greece became Orthodox and still are. In 1453 the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople and turned Hagia Sophia into a mosque. Today the building still stands, and Orthodox churches in Chicago neighborhoods still use domes and icons that look back to it.

words.d: a picture made from many tiny pieces of colored glass or stone
the branch of Christianity centered in the Greek-speaking East, with the patriarch of Constantinople
a formal split between two groups that once belonged together
the head bishop of a major Eastern Christian church

look.title: A Historian Looks Up
look.text: Procopius, who worked for Justinian, described the new church for readers who had never seen it. He wrote that the dome did not seem to rest on the walls beneath it but seemed to hang from heaven by a golden chain, and that the light inside seemed to come from within the building itself.
look.prompt: Procopius worked for the emperor. Does that make his praise less useful as evidence, or does it still tell us something true?

check.q: Why does the dome of Hagia Sophia seem to float?
choices: A ring of forty windows at its base lets light pour in
It is not attached to the building
It is painted blue like the sky
check.why: The windows around the base of the dome flood it with light, hiding the supports from view.

check.q: What was the schism of 1054?
choices: A riot that burned the city
The formal split between the Orthodox and Catholic churches
The building of a new alphabet
check.why: The patriarch of Constantinople and the pope in Rome broke with each other, and the churches remain separate.

check.q: Which countries became Orthodox partly through Byzantine missionaries?
check.why: Cyril and Methodius and later missionaries brought Orthodox Christianity to the Slavic lands.

lessons.title: A Merchant in Mecca
lessons.mainIdea: Islam began in the trading city of Mecca in the early 600s, when Muhammad taught that there is one God and that all believers are equal before him.
reading: Arabia in the year 600 was mostly desert. Its people lived in tribes, raising camels and sheep or trading along the caravan roads. Mecca was a trading town near the Red Sea coast. It also held a shrine, the Kaaba, that drew pilgrims from all over Arabia. They came to honor many gods and to buy and sell. Feuds between tribes were common, and a person without a strong family had little protection.

Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570. His parents died when he was young, and an uncle raised him. He became a merchant, known as honest. Around 610, when he was about forty, he began to report visions in which an angel gave him messages from God. He taught that there is only one God, the same God worshiped by Jews and Christians, and that people should care for the poor, the orphan and the widow. His followers memorized his messages, which were later gathered into the *Quran*, the holy book of Islam.

The leaders of Mecca did not like this teaching. It insulted their gods and threatened their pilgrim trade. They harassed Muhammad's followers. In 622 he and his followers left for the town of Yathrib, later called Medina. This journey is the *hijra*, and Muslims count their calendar from that year. In Medina, Muhammad became a leader of the community and settled disputes among its tribes.

By the time Muhammad died in 632, most of Arabia had accepted Islam. The word Islam means submission to God, and a *Muslim* is one who submits. The faith asked five main duties of every believer: to declare that there is one God and Muhammad is his messenger, to pray five times a day, to give to the poor, to fast during the month of Ramadan, and, if able, to make the pilgrimage to Mecca once in life. Every duty was the same for a rich man and a poor one.

words.d: the holy book of Islam, believed by Muslims to be God's words given to Muhammad
the move of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622, year one of the Muslim calendar
a follower of Islam; the word means one who submits to God
a journey to a holy place for religious reasons

look.title: The Same Rules for Everyone
look.text: Imagine a town where a rich merchant and a poor camel driver both stop work at the same hour, face the same direction and say the same prayer, then both give a share of what they own to the poor. Before this, the town honored dozens of gods, and a person's worth depended on his tribe.
look.prompt: Why might this teaching appeal to poorer people and worry the town's richest families?

check.q: Why did Mecca's leaders oppose Muhammad?
choices: He wanted to move the Kaaba
His message insulted their gods and threatened the pilgrim trade
He refused to be a merchant
check.why: Muhammad's teaching of one God threatened both Mecca's religion and the business pilgrims brought.

check.q: From what event does the Muslim calendar count its years?
choices: The hijra, the move to Medina in 622
check.why: The hijra of 622 is year one of the Muslim calendar.

check.q: What do the five duties have in common?
choices: They apply equally to rich and poor believers
They must all be done in Mecca
check.why: Prayer, giving, fasting, pilgrimage and the declaration of faith were the same for every Muslim.

lessons.title: Caliphs and a Growing Empire
lessons.mainIdea: Within a century of Muhammad's death, Muslim rulers called caliphs governed lands from Spain to India, ruling many peoples who kept their own faiths.
reading: When Muhammad died, his followers chose a leader called a *caliph*, meaning successor. The first four caliphs ruled from Medina. Their armies moved fast. The Byzantine and Persian empires had worn each other out in long wars, and their people were heavily taxed. Arab armies took Syria, Egypt and Persia within twenty years. Many local people did not fight hard for the old rulers.

A family called the Umayyads took the caliphate in 661 and moved the capital to Damascus in Syria. Under them the empire reached Spain in the west and the Indus River in the east by about 750. Then a rival family, the Abbasids, overthrew them. The Abbasids built a new capital in 762 on the Tigris River: Baghdad. Within a century it was one of the largest cities in the world, a round city of palaces, markets and canals.

Ruling so many peoples took more than swords. Christians and Jews were called People of the Book, because they too had scriptures. They could keep their religion and their churches if they paid a special tax. Many did, and for centuries most people in Egypt and Syria remained Christian. Over time many converted, partly because Muslims paid less tax and could rise in government.

The empire was never fully united. Spain broke away under its own Umayyad ruler. Later, other rulers in Egypt and North Africa claimed the title too. Even so, from Cordoba in Spain to Samarkand in Central Asia, people shared Arabic as the language of learning and law, the same coins, and the same duty to travel to Mecca. That shared world is what let a king from Mali cross it in 1324.

words.d: a ruler of the Muslim community after Muhammad; the word means successor
the lands and government ruled by a caliph
to change from one religion to another

look.title: How Fast the Caliphate Grew
look.prompt: About how many years passed between Muhammad's death and the arrival of Muslim armies in Spain? Why might that speed surprise people?

check.q: Why did Arab armies conquer Syria, Egypt and Persia so quickly?
choices: The Byzantine and Persian empires were exhausted by war and their people heavily taxed
check.why: Long wars had weakened both old empires, and many of their subjects did not fight hard to keep them.

check.q: Where did the Abbasids build their new capital in 762?
check.why: The Abbasids built Baghdad on the Tigris River, and it became one of the world's largest cities.

check.q: How were Christians and Jews treated under the early caliphs?
choices: They were forced to convert at once
They were expelled from the empire
They could keep their faith if they paid a special tax
check.why: As People of the Book, they kept their religion and paid a tax; many converted only over centuries.

lessons.title: The House of Wisdom
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars in Baghdad gathered the knowledge of Greece, Persia and India, and added algebra, new astronomy and medicine that Europe later learned from them.
reading: In the early 800s the caliph al-Ma'mun paid scholars in Baghdad to collect books. Greek, Persian and Indian works were translated into Arabic. Historians call this effort the *House of Wisdom*. It was part library, part translation office, part research center. Christian, Jewish and Muslim scholars worked there together. Paper, a Chinese invention, had recently reached the Muslim world, and it made books far cheaper than parchment.

One scholar, Muhammad al-Khwarizmi, wrote a book around 820 on solving problems with unknown numbers. Its title used the Arabic word al-jabr, and from that we get the word *algebra*. He also explained the number system from India, which used ten symbols and a zero. We still call them Arabic numerals because Europe learned them from Arabic books. The word algorithm, a set of steps for solving a problem, comes from his name.

Astronomers built observatories and measured the positions of stars more carefully than the Greeks had. They improved the *astrolabe*, a brass instrument that finds the time and one's position from the stars. Muslims needed it to know the hour of prayer and the direction of Mecca, and sailors needed it at sea. Many star names we still use, like Aldebaran and Rigel, are Arabic.

A Persian physician, Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, wrote a huge medical textbook around 1025. Doctors in Europe used it for five hundred years. Hospitals in Baghdad and Cairo treated patients of any religion. When European scholars in the 1100s wanted Aristotle, Euclid or the latest medicine, they went to Spain to translate it from Arabic. Much of ancient Greek science survived because Baghdad had saved it.

words.d: the library and translation center in Baghdad in the 800s where scholars gathered and studied the world's knowledge
math that solves for unknown numbers; from the Arabic word al-jabr
a brass instrument that uses the stars to find the time and one's position
to put words from one language into another

look.title: Numbers Before Zero
look.text: Try to multiply 48 by 23 using only Roman numerals: XLVIII times XXIII. There is no zero and no column for tens or hundreds. Now do it with the ten symbols from India: 48 times 23, lining up the digits. Merchants in Baghdad switched to the new system for a reason.
look.prompt: Why would a number system with a zero and place value matter to a tax collector, a merchant or an astronomer?

check.q: Where does the word algebra come from?
choices: The Arabic word al-jabr in al-Khwarizmi's book title
The name of a Persian city
check.why: Al-Khwarizmi's book on solving for unknowns used the word al-jabr, which became algebra.

check.q: Why were the numerals we use called Arabic numerals?
choices: Europe learned them from Arabic books, though they came from India
They were first used in Mecca
They were only used in Arabia
check.why: The system came from India; Europeans met it through Arabic works like al-Khwarizmi's.

check.q: How did ancient Greek science reach medieval Europe?
choices: Through Arabic translations, later put into Latin in Spain
Greek books were kept in Paris the whole time
check.why: Baghdad's scholars saved Greek works in Arabic, and Europeans translated them from Arabic in the 1100s.

sections.title: Gold and Salt Across the Sahara

lessons.title: The Ship of the Desert
lessons.mainIdea: The camel turned the Sahara from a wall into a road, and along that road salt went south while gold went north.
reading: The Sahara is the largest hot desert on earth, about the size of the United States. Crossing it from north to south meant weeks of sand, rock and heat with water only at scattered oases. Horses and donkeys died. Then, around the 300s CE, herders in North Africa began using the *camel*, brought from Arabia. A camel can carry several hundred pounds and go a week or more without drinking. It can close its nostrils against sand. Traders called it the ship of the desert.

A trading trip was a *caravan*: dozens or hundreds of camels, guides who knew the wells, and armed guards. The main route ran from Sijilmasa in Morocco south to the Niger River, roughly a thousand miles, taking about two months. Caravans traveled by night in the hottest season and steered by the stars. A lost caravan was a dead one, and the desert is scattered with old bones to prove it.

The trade worked because each side had what the other lacked. In the middle of the desert, at a place called Taghaza, workers cut slabs of salt from the ground like stone. The lands south of the desert had almost no salt, and people and animals cannot live without it. South of the desert, in the forests along rivers, people dug gold from the earth. North Africa and Europe wanted that gold for coins. Salt went south, gold went north.

Traders also carried copper, cloth, horses and books south, and brought ivory, kola nuts and enslaved people north. Along with the goods came Islam. Merchants from North Africa were Muslims, and they settled in the trading towns south of the desert. Over centuries, kings and city people there adopted the faith, learned Arabic and built mosques. Village farmers often kept older beliefs much longer.

words.d: a desert animal that can carry heavy loads and go days without water
a group of traders and pack animals traveling together for safety
a place in the desert where water reaches the surface and plants grow
the vast desert across North Africa, about the size of the United States

look.title: Numbers for a Crossing
rows: Distance, Sijilmasa to the Niger, about (miles)
Load one camel can carry, about (pounds)
Days a camel can go without water, about
look.prompt: Using these numbers, about how many miles a day did a caravan travel? Why would traders risk such a trip for salt and gold?

check.q: What changed to make crossing the Sahara possible on a large scale?
choices: Rivers were dug across the desert
The camel arrived in North Africa
check.why: Camels could carry heavy loads and go days without water, unlike horses and donkeys.

check.q: Why did people south of the Sahara pay gold for salt?
choices: Salt was rare in their lands and they could not live without it
Salt was used to make gold coins
They had too much gold to store
check.why: Their region had almost no salt, and every person and animal needs it, while gold was plentiful nearby.

check.q: How did Islam spread south of the Sahara?
choices: Caliphs sent armies across the desert
Muslim merchants settled in trading towns and rulers adopted the faith over time
Everyone converted in a single year
check.why: Islam traveled with trade; kings and townspeople adopted it, while many farmers kept older beliefs longer.

lessons.title: Ghana, the Land of Gold
lessons.mainIdea: The kingdom of Ghana grew rich by taxing the salt and gold that crossed its land, and we know about it mainly from Arab writers.
reading: The first great kingdom on the southern edge of the Sahara was Ghana. It lay in what is now Mali and Mauritania, far northwest of the modern country named Ghana, which took the old name in 1957. Ghana's people, the Soninke, controlled the strip of land between the salt mines to the north and the gold fields to the south. Every trader had to pass through, and every load paid a tax coming in and going out.

Almost everything we know about Ghana comes from writers in the Muslim world who never saw it. The best is al-Bakri, a scholar in Spain, who in 1068 wrote down what traders told him. He described the capital as two towns six miles apart: one for Muslim merchants with a dozen mosques, and one for the king, with his palace and his own religion's shrines. The king sat in a pavilion with gold-decked horses and dogs in gold collars. Al-Bakri said the king could put a huge army into the field.

The king kept control of gold with a clever rule. All nuggets found in the kingdom belonged to him. People could keep only gold dust. This kept nuggets from flooding the market and made gold stay valuable. Al-Bakri also reported that a load of salt paid one gold coin entering and two leaving. This is a tax on trade, and it is the source of Ghana's wealth.

Ghana had no written records of its own that survive, so historians are careful. Al-Bakri's numbers came from travelers and may be stretched. But archaeologists have dug a large stone town at a site called Koumbi Saleh in Mauritania that matches his description of the merchant town. By the 1200s Ghana had weakened, hurt by attacks from the north and by new gold fields opening farther south, outside its control.

words.d: the people who built the kingdom of Ghana
a payment a government requires from people or from trade
a scientist who studies the past by digging up and studying what people left behind

look.title: A Scholar in Spain Describes a King He Never Met
look.text: Al-Bakri wrote that the king of Ghana held court in a domed pavilion, surrounded by ten horses covered in gold cloth. Behind him stood the sons of lesser kings, dressed in fine cloth with gold braided into their hair. The door was guarded by dogs of the best breed, wearing collars of gold and silver. He added that all gold nuggets found in the land went to the king, and only gold dust was left for the people.
look.cite: al-Bakri, Book of Routes and Realms, 1068 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Al-Bakri got this from traders. What parts of the report would a trader know well, and what parts might be exaggerated?

check.q: Where did Ghana's wealth come from?
choices: Its own gold mines in the capital
Taxing the salt and gold that crossed its land
check.why: Ghana sat between the salt and the gold and taxed every load that passed through.

check.q: Why did the king keep all gold nuggets for himself?
choices: He used them to build his palace
To keep gold scarce and valuable
check.why: If nuggets flooded the market, gold would be worth less; keeping them limited the supply.

check.q: What evidence supports al-Bakri's description of Ghana's capital?
choices: A film of the king's court
Ruins of a large stone town dug up at Koumbi Saleh
check.why: Archaeologists found a stone merchant town in Mauritania that matches al-Bakri's account.

lessons.title: Mali, Mansa Musa and Timbuktu
lessons.mainIdea: The Empire of Mali replaced Ghana, and under Mansa Musa its wealth and its city of Timbuktu became famous across Africa and Europe.
reading: Around 1235 a leader named Sundiata united the Mande people and defeated a rival king in battle. He founded the Empire of *Mali*, which grew to include the old lands of Ghana and the new gold fields to the south. Storytellers called griots have passed down Sundiata's story by memory for nearly eight hundred years. It is one of the great epics of Africa, and it is also a source historians use, carefully, alongside written records.

Mali's most famous ruler, Mansa Musa, took the throne around 1312. *Mansa* means ruler or king. His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 was the event you read about at the start of this chapter. On his way home he brought back scholars, architects and books. He had mosques built in Timbuktu and Gao. Fifty years later a mapmaker in Spain drew the Catalan Atlas and showed Mansa Musa sitting on a throne in the middle of Africa, holding a gold nugget. Europe now knew where the gold came from.

Timbuktu sat where the Niger River came closest to the desert. Salt caravans from the north and boats of grain and gold from the south met there. By the 1400s it had a university based at the Sankore mosque, and scholars wrote and copied books on law, religion, math and astronomy. Families in Timbuktu still keep thousands of these old manuscripts today. They prove that West Africa had a written learned tradition long before Europeans arrived.

The traveler Ibn Battuta visited Mali in 1352 and 1353. He praised the safety of its roads and the fairness of its judges. He also complained about customs he found strange and about the small gifts he received. His account is valuable because he was an outsider who saw things the empire's own people would not bother to write down. By the 1400s Mali weakened, and the empire of Songhai took over Timbuktu.

words.d: the West African empire founded by Sundiata around 1235 that grew rich from gold
the title of the ruler of Mali; it means king
a West African storyteller and musician who keeps history by memory
a book or document written by hand

look.title: A Traveler Judges Mali
look.text: Ibn Battuta wrote that the people of Mali rarely did wrong, and that their ruler punished injustice more than any other. He said that a traveler in their country had no fear of thieves, and that a stranger who died there had his goods kept safely by trusted men until his family could claim them.
look.cite: Ibn Battuta, Travels, describing his visit of 1352–1353 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Ibn Battuta had traveled across Asia and Africa. Why would a merchant reading this want to trade in Mali?

check.q: Who founded the Empire of Mali?
check.why: Sundiata united the Mande people around 1235; Mansa Musa ruled later, in the early 1300s.

check.q: What do the manuscripts kept in Timbuktu prove?
choices: West Africa had a written tradition of learning before Europeans arrived
check.why: Thousands of hand-written books on law, math and astronomy show a long scholarly tradition.

check.q: Why is Ibn Battuta's account of Mali especially useful?
choices: He was the king's official historian
He was an outsider who noticed things locals would not write down
He lived in Mali his whole life
check.why: Outsiders often record everyday things that seem too ordinary for insiders to mention.

sections.title: Stone Cities of the South and East

lessons.title: Great Zimbabwe
lessons.mainIdea: In southern Africa, the builders of Great Zimbabwe raised huge stone walls and traded gold to the coast, and their ruins later exposed a racist lie.
reading: On a high plateau in southern Africa stand the stone walls of *Great Zimbabwe*. The word zimbabwe means houses of stone in the Shona language. The largest structure, the Great Enclosure, has curved walls up to about 36 feet high and as much as 16 feet thick, built from cut granite blocks laid without mortar. Inside stands a solid stone tower shaped like a cone. Between about 1100 and 1450, this was the capital of a kingdom of the Shona people.

The rulers of Great Zimbabwe raised cattle and controlled gold mines on the plateau. Gold went east, to the coast, and goods came back. Archaeologists digging inside the walls have found glass beads from India, pieces of Persian pottery and Chinese porcelain. A coin from the Swahili city of Kilwa turned up there too. A city with no writing left records anyway: the things it bought tell us who it traded with.

Historians estimate that ten thousand or more people lived in and around the walls at the city's height. The walls do not look like a fort. There are no towers for archers. Instead they seem built to show power, to separate the ruler's family from everyone else. Soapstone carvings of birds, found on the site, are now the symbol of the modern nation of Zimbabwe. Sometime in the 1400s the city was abandoned, perhaps because grazing land and firewood ran out.

For a long time, white settlers and colonial officials refused to believe Africans had built it. They claimed it was the work of ancient Phoenicians or a lost white race. Archaeologists who dug there in the early 1900s, including a British scholar named Gertrude Caton-Thompson in 1929, showed clearly that the builders were local Africans. The government of the colony then called Rhodesia still tried to suppress that finding for decades. The stones did not lie, but some people did.

words.d: the stone capital of a Shona kingdom in southern Africa, about 1100 to 1450
a large area of high, mostly flat land
a paste used to hold stones or bricks together
the people of the Zimbabwe plateau who built Great Zimbabwe

choices: Chinese porcelain, Indian beads and a Kilwa coin found in the ruins
A map painted on the tower

check.q: Why do historians think the walls were not mainly a fort?

check.why: The walls lack any defensive features, so they seem meant to display power and separate the ruler's family.

check.q: What did colonial officials claim about Great Zimbabwe, and why was it wrong?

That it was too small to matter; it was huge

lessons.title: The Swahili Coast
lessons.mainIdea: Along Africa's east coast, city-states like Kilwa grew rich on Indian Ocean trade and blended African, Arab and Persian ways into Swahili culture.
reading: The Indian Ocean has a gift for sailors: the *monsoon* winds. For half the year they blow from Africa toward India, and for the other half they blow back. A ship could ride one wind out and the other home. Sailors from Arabia, Persia and India had used these winds for centuries. By the 800s they were trading regularly with towns along the coast of East Africa, in what are now Somalia, Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique.

Those towns became *city-states*, each with its own ruler. Mogadishu, Mombasa, Zanzibar and Kilwa were the best known. The people were African, mainly Bantu-speaking, but merchants from Arabia and Persia settled among them, married local women and brought Islam. The mix produced the *Swahili* language and culture. Swahili is a Bantu language with many Arabic words, and it is still spoken by tens of millions of people in East Africa today.

Kilwa, an island off Tanzania, controlled the gold coming from the Zimbabwe plateau. Its rulers built a palace of coral stone with a swimming pool, and a great mosque with domes. Kilwa minted its own copper coins. Ibn Battuta stopped there in 1331 and called it one of the most beautiful and well-built towns he had seen. Its merchants sold gold, ivory and enslaved people, and bought cloth, porcelain and glass.

In the early 1400s the Chinese admiral Zheng He sailed fleets of huge ships across the Indian Ocean and reached the Swahili coast. A ruler there sent a giraffe back to the Chinese emperor as a gift. Then in 1498 Portuguese ships rounded the southern tip of Africa and arrived at the coast. Within a few years they had bombarded Kilwa and Mombasa. The old trading world of the Indian Ocean would never be the same.

words.d: a wind that blows one way for half the year and the opposite way for the other half
a city that rules itself and the land around it, like a small country
the language and culture of the East African coast, blending Bantu roots with Arabic words and Islam

look.title: Waiting for the Wind
look.text: A merchant from Arabia lands at Kilwa in December on the northeast wind. The wind will not turn around until about April. For four months he lives in the town, eats its food, learns its words and does business face to face. Many merchants married there and stayed.
look.prompt: How would the monsoon calendar, which forced traders to stay for months, help create a blended culture like Swahili?

check.q: How did the monsoon winds help Indian Ocean trade?
choices: They blew one way for half the year and back for the other half
They kept ships in port all year
check.why: Sailors rode the wind out and waited for it to reverse to sail home.

check.q: What is the Swahili language?
choices: A Bantu language with many Arabic words
check.why: Swahili grew from Bantu roots as Arab and Persian merchants settled among African communities.

check.q: What did Kilwa control that made it rich?
choices: The gold trade from the Zimbabwe plateau
check.why: Gold from the interior passed through Kilwa on its way to Arabia, India and beyond.

lessons.title: A Connected World
lessons.mainIdea: Between 500 and 1500, goods, faiths and ideas moved along linked routes across Africa, Asia and Europe, and the trade had winners and victims.
reading: Put the pieces of this chapter on one map. A camel caravan carries gold north from Mali to Morocco. A ship carries it to Cairo, where it is struck into coins. Byzantine merchants and Italian traders carry those coins to Constantinople and Venice. Meanwhile, gold from Zimbabwe goes east through Kilwa, across the ocean to India, and on to China. Paper from China reaches Baghdad, then Cairo, then Timbuktu. No single trader went all the way. But the routes connected, link by link.

Ideas moved along with goods. Islam traveled with merchants to West Africa and the Swahili coast. Greek science, saved in Arabic in Baghdad, reached Spain and then European universities. The numerals from India reached Europe through Arabic books. A student in Timbuktu and a student in Cordoba might study the same law book. A doctor in Paris in the 1300s read a Persian textbook. Religion, math and medicine crossed deserts and oceans.

The same routes carried people who had no choice. The trans-Saharan trade and the Indian Ocean trade both moved enslaved Africans north and east, to Egypt, Arabia, Persia and India, over many centuries. Al-Bakri, Ibn Battuta and Kilwa's merchants all mention it plainly. Later, from the 1500s on, European ships would carry a far larger number of enslaved Africans west across the Atlantic. The history of trade is also a history of who paid its price.

By about 1450 this connected world was ready for something new. Sailors on the Swahili coast and the Atlantic coast of Morocco knew the winds. Maps in Spain showed where Mali's gold lay. The Ottoman Turks were about to take Constantinople and its trade routes. Portuguese captains were pushing down the coast of Africa. The next chapter turns to Europe, the Mongols and the Americas, and the world that was about to collide.

words.d: a regular path that travelers or traders follow
forced to work as another person's property, with no freedom

look.title: Following One Sheet of Paper
look.text: A sheet of paper is made in a Chinese workshop around 750. Paper-making spreads to Samarkand, then Baghdad, then Cairo. By the 1300s scholars in Timbuktu write on paper carried across the Sahara by camel. Before paper, a book meant animal skin, and a single copy of a long book could cost as much as a farm.
look.prompt: How could a cheaper way to make a page change who got to learn to read?

check.q: How did gold from Mali reach Constantinople?
choices: One trader carried it the whole way by camel
Through a chain of separate traders: caravan, ship, then merchants
check.why: No single merchant went all the way; the routes linked up and goods changed hands many times.

check.q: Which idea traveled from India through Arabic books to Europe?
choices: The numerals with zero and place value
check.why: Al-Khwarizmi explained the Indian number system, and Europe learned it from Arabic works.

choices: Because enslaved people were carried along the same routes as gold and salt
check.why: The Saharan and Indian Ocean routes moved enslaved Africans for centuries, as the sources say plainly.

review.q: Which empire lasted from 330 to 1453 with its capital at Constantinople?
review.why: The eastern Roman Empire, called Byzantine, lasted more than eleven hundred years.

review.q: What was Justinian's most lasting achievement?
choices: Organizing Roman law into one code
review.why: His Code sorted a thousand years of law and still influences legal systems today.

review.q: In what year did the hijra take place, beginning the Muslim calendar?
review.why: Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina in 622.

review.q: What work was done at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad?
choices: Translating and studying Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge
Building ships for the Indian Ocean
review.why: Scholars there translated ancient works and made new advances in math, astronomy and medicine.

review.q: What two goods drove the trans-Saharan trade?
review.why: Salt from the desert went south, and gold from the forest lands went north.

review.q: Why did the price of gold fall in Cairo after 1324?
choices: Mansa Musa brought and gave away so much gold that the supply rose
review.why: A sudden flood of gold made each piece worth less, and prices stayed low for years.

review.q: How do we know Great Zimbabwe traded with the Indian Ocean world?
choices: Its kings wrote letters to China
Chinese, Persian and Indian goods were found inside its walls
Its walls are made of coral
review.why: Objects from far away, dug up at the site, are the evidence; the city left no writing.

choices: A blend of African, Arab and Persian ways formed by trade
Pure Arabian culture moved to Africa
A Chinese colony on the coast
review.why: Merchants from across the ocean settled among Bantu-speaking Africans, producing a new language and culture.
